title: Shooting Stars Aren't Stars at All

youtube.title: Shooting Stars Aren't Stars (Leonids 2026) | Dig Deeper
youtube.description: What are shooting stars really? The Leonid meteor shower 2026 peaks on the night of November 17, and every streak you see is a tiny crumb of comet dust hitting our air at 71 km per second. Find out where shooting stars come from, why they glow, and the crazy night in 1966 when the sky rained thousands of meteors per minute.

scenes.narration: Every shooting star you've ever wished on was probably smaller than a grain of sand.

Yes, really. I'm Sir Digsworth, and I can tell you that shooting stars aren't stars at all. They're tiny crumbs of space dust. And next week, a whole shower of them is coming. But the craziest part is what happened in 1966, so do stick around.
So where do these crumbs come from? Meet comet Tempel Tuttle.
Every time it swings past the Sun, it heats up and sheds a trail of dust and pebbles. Like a messy kid leaving cookie crumbs all over the house.
And every November, Earth plows straight through that trail. That's the Leonid meteor shower.

fact.label: Did you know?
fact.text: Every November, Earth passes through dust left behind by comet Tempel-Tuttle.

scenes.narration: And these crumbs are fast. Like, ridiculously fast. Seventy one kilometers per second.
At that speed, you could fly all the way around the Earth in under four minutes.

fact.label: Speed check
fact.text: At 71 km/s you could circle the whole Earth in under 4 minutes!

scenes.narration: When a crumb slams into the air about a hundred kilometers above your head, it squeezes the air in front of it so hard that it heats up and glows. That bright streak is the shooting star.
And no, it won't land on your head. These grains are so tiny that they burn up completely, long before they get anywhere near the ground.
Okay, 1966. Most years you can spot maybe ten to fifteen Leonids an hour. But one night in 1966, people saw thousands of meteors per minute, for about fifteen minutes straight.

fact.label: The 1966 storm
fact.text: Thousands of meteors per MINUTE, for about 15 minutes!

scenes.narration: Why? Earth smashed into an extra thick clump of fresh comet dust. These meteor storms tend to happen about every thirty three years, when the comet swings back around.
The comet comes back in 2031, so the years around then are our best shot at another storm.
But you can still catch some this year. The peak is the night of November seventeenth. Go somewhere dark after midnight, look up, and give your eyes about twenty minutes to adjust.
So, a quick recap. Shooting stars are tiny comet crumbs, moving terribly fast and glowing a hundred kilometers up. Subscribe, and next time, Sir Digsworth digs even deeper.
